title: How leaders drive AI adoption: what 485 post-coaching comments show
summary: We read a year of post-coaching 360 feedback. Colleagues described leaders building AI fluency, running experiments and bringing teams through change.
body_markdown:
Most companies now have AI tools. Far fewer have teams that use them well. The gap is rarely the licence or the training module. It is usually what happens around a leader: whether they try the tools themselves, whether they make it safe for people to experiment, and whether they bring the team along at a pace it can absorb.


We wanted to know what that looks like in practice, so Torch’s Client Success team read a year of written feedback from the people who work with our coached leaders. This article shares what they found. It is written for HR and talent leaders who are being asked to help their organisation adopt AI and want to know which leadership behaviours to develop.


## Key takeaways


- In one year of post-coaching feedback, colleagues and leaders wrote 485 comments describing change in how coached leaders handled AI or innovation: 136 about AI and automation, and 349 about innovation more broadly.
- 83% of those comments came from colleagues (peers, managers, direct reports and cross-functional partners) rather than from the leaders themselves. The change was visible to other people.
- The most common AI pattern was a leader **using the tools personally and helping the team do the same** (57 comments). Close behind were **leading people through AI-driven change** (41) and **redesigning work with automation** (38).
- On innovation, the largest theme was **building a culture of experimentation** (86 comments), followed by generating and championing new ideas (75).
- Several leaders described the same lesson: adoption moves faster when you meet people where they are, rather than pushing urgency onto them.
- This is qualitative evidence of what people observed after coaching. It is not a rate, and it does not prove coaching caused the change.


## What we looked at


Torch programmes end with a[360 Impact reassessment](https://torch.io/products/custom-360/) . Each leader’s manager, peers, direct reports and other colleagues are asked, capacity by capacity, whether they have seen *no change* or *improvement* since coaching began, and then to describe what they saw in their own words. Leaders also write a self-reflection on what they learned and how it changed their work.


The team read every completed 360 Impact written response from December 2025 to November 2026, and every Coaching Experience Survey answer since March 2025 to the question about insights and progress after the first three sessions. They screened for AI, automation, named tools, innovation, experimentation and related ideas. They also read every answer to the innovation capacity questions and every self-reflection in full, so comments that never used a keyword were still found.


Only comments describing a change counted. Where a colleague rated a capacity, only *Improved* ratings were included; 100 *No change* ratings were set aside. The final set was 485 comments (428 positive and 57 mixed) about 262 leaders, working with 147 coaches across 52 client organisations.


## Nine patterns in how leaders changed


Theme Comments


**AI:** championing AI adoption and fluency 57


**AI:** leading people through AI-driven change 41


**AI:** reimagining work with AI and automation 38


Building a culture of experimentation 86


Generating and championing new ideas 75


Curiosity and openness 59


Leading transformation and change 55


Turning ideas into action 54


Future-focused strategic thinking 20


Each comment was assigned one main theme. Comments touching both AI and innovation were filed under AI.


### 1. They use the tools themselves, then make room for the team


The most common AI theme was not a strategy announcement. It was a leader visibly learning. A skip-level manager wrote that a leader “has taken initiative to set up Claude Code on his workstation and is actively learning how to leverage AI tools to enhance his productivity.”


The best examples paired enthusiasm with judgment. One manager described a leader who “has really embraced LLM-assisted spec’ing and coding while maintaining healthy skepticism. He’s adopting new tools with optimism and encouraging the team not to hand over all critical thinking to AI.”


That balance matters for buyers. A leader who adopts tools uncritically can create as much risk as one who ignores them. What colleagues valued was a leader who tried things openly and set a sensible standard for how the team should use them.


### 2. They slow down for people so adoption can speed up


The comments about leading people through AI-driven change kept returning to pace. One leader wrote in their self-reflection:


> “To drive meaningful change, I need to meet people where they are emotionally rather than pushing them into AI adoption before they’re ready. This means trading my sense of urgency for genuine curiosity—asking thoughtful questions and helping them see the narrative of opportunity and wins, rather than focusing on what they’re missing.”


A direct report described the same quality from the other side, saying their manager “builds the bridge that helps people adapt to change at a pace that works for them.” Another wrote that since the team began using AI, their leader had “become even more efficient while also making sure to bring all of us along.”


This is the part of AI adoption that tool training cannot reach. It is a leadership conversation about fear, status and workload, and it is exactly the kind of conversation coaching prepares people for.


### 3. They redesign work, not just tasks


The automation theme was the most concrete. One leader described partnering with a data team “to automate consumption revenue reporting, eliminating two days of monthly manual work,” and said coaching had helped them “shift from being primarily execution-focused to operating more strategically.”


A peer described a leader who “built an automated coaching skill grounded in our team’s core precepts, giving colleagues a way to self-serve on their own improvement opportunities.” The value there was not the tool. It was a leader turning what the team already knew into something everyone could use.


### 4. They make experimentation normal


The largest theme overall was building a culture of experimentation, with 86 comments. One participant summed up their shift as “not confining myself to a box of options or capabilities and treating the workplace like a lab for experiments.”


Another wrote that the most valuable lesson from coaching was that “asking the right questions is far more effective than providing the right answers,” and that guiding people toward their own solutions had “strengthened accountability, boosted engagement, and fostered a culture of continuous improvement.”


For AI adoption, this is the foundation. Teams try new tools when trying something and getting it wrong is treated as normal work, not a risk to their reputation.


### 5. They use AI to lead better, not only to work faster


A few of the most interesting comments were about AI supporting the leader’s own development. One leader described a tense exchange where they “paused rather than reacting defensively,” took time to regulate their emotions, and “then used AI to help draft a thoughtful response that clearly explained my reasoning while genuinely inviting their input.”


Another said their coach “even suggested I use tools like Claude to reframe pointed questions before I send them.” A third summed up their takeaway as: “Take action in bite-size pieces. Use AI to supplement knowledge and start small vs. waiting for time to do something bigger.”


## Why colleagues’ views matter most


Self-reported change is useful, but it is easy to discount. In this set, 404 of the 485 comments came from colleagues. Within the 360 Impact alone, the share was 93%. Peers wrote 104 comments, cross-functional partners 97, direct reports 81 and managers 78.


That spread matters. AI adoption happens across team boundaries, so a leader’s peers and partners are often the first to notice whether that leader is making new ways of working easier or harder.


## What HR and talent leaders can take from this


1. **Develop the leadership behaviours, not only the tool skills.** The most common patterns here are personal adoption, pacing change for people and making experimentation safe. A prompt-writing course does not build those.
2. **Ask colleagues what changed.** Self-assessment alone will miss most of the signal. Use a 360 with an explicit “since coaching began” question and a no-change option.
3. **Measure against your own framework.** The leaders in this set were rated on capacities such as adaptive mindset, innovation enablement and strategic foresight. Choose the capacities your AI strategy actually needs, then ask about those.
4. **Keep the claims honest.** This kind of evidence shows what people observed. Pair it with operating measures, such as tool usage or cycle time, before claiming business impact.


## What this evidence does and does not show


This is a qualitative review, chosen to find AI and innovation behaviour. It shows what colleagues and leaders described after coaching. It does not show what share of all coached leaders changed, because comments outside these topics were not counted. It does not prove that coaching caused the change: these leaders were also working in organisations that were investing in AI. Quotations are lightly edited for anonymity; leaders, colleagues and client organisations are not named.

## Frequently asked questions


### What leadership behaviours help AI adoption?


In this review, the most common were leaders using AI tools themselves and helping their team do the same, pacing change so people could adapt, redesigning work with automation, and making experimentation safe. Colleagues noticed these more than any formal announcement.


### Does coaching help leaders adopt AI?


Colleagues of coached leaders described changes in AI use and innovation in 485 comments over a year. That is evidence of observed change after coaching, not proof that coaching caused it. Organisations should pair it with their own adoption and performance measures.


### How was the feedback collected?


From Torch’s 360 Impact reassessment at the end of coaching, where colleagues rate each capacity as improved or unchanged and explain what they saw, plus participant surveys after the first three coaching sessions. Only comments describing a change were counted.


### Why use colleague feedback rather than self-assessment?


Leaders tend to judge their own change differently from the people around them. Colleagues see whether new behaviour shows up in meetings, decisions and handoffs. In this set, 83% of the comments came from colleagues.


### How do I measure AI leadership on my own framework?


Choose the capacities your AI strategy depends on, write behaviour-based questions for each, include a “since coaching began” question with a no-change option, and use the same instrument before and after. Then compare the results with operating measures.
